text: Which EU-funded projects study how nineteenth-century companies and business groups tried to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopted?

The match is an unpunctuated work-stream list in one report block; the relevant stream is 'the efforts of social actors, including water companies, municipalities, private entrepreneurs, technicians and users, to regulate access, use and distribution of water in 19th-century italian cities' - water supply governance with companies as one participant among users and municipalities, not business groups seeking to influence the policies a government adopts. The verb 'shap' in that block belongs to a different stream ('water use rights shaped economic policy ... during the 17th and 18th centuries').

absence_evidence.sql: WITH t AS (SELECT p.id, p.acronym, lower(p.objective || ' ' || COALESCE(r.rt,'')) AS txt FROM project p LEFT JOIN (SELECT projectID, string_agg(COALESCE(teaser,'')||' '||COALESCE(summary,'')||' '||COALESCE(workPerformed,'')||' '||COALESCE(finalResults,''), ' ') AS rt FROM report_text GROUP BY projectID) r ON r.projectID = p.id) SELECT id, acronym FROM t WHERE regexp_matches(txt,'merchant') AND regexp_matches(txt,'petition') AND regexp_matches(txt,'(city council|parliament|free trade)') ORDER BY id
absence_evidence.key_result: The corpus does hold business-influence-on-government history - in another century: 101025880 PETITIA studies 'Why did Dutch merchants petition the Amsterdam city council for free trade in the English Empire' and situates it as the origin of transnational advocacy networks 'predating the nineteenth century' (seventeenth century). The other row, 762458 Waste Compactor, is a keyword coincidence.

reference_answer: No EU-funded project in this corpus studies nineteenth-century business or corporate efforts to influence government policy; nothing matches this question. The corpus's research on business influence over policy is contemporary or late-twentieth-century (BUSWEL, PROSPER, TRASC, BIZPOL, EFTA DEVELOPMENT on 1958-1992), and its nineteenth-century projects (TRANSPOP on popular politics, WARCAP on fiscal capacity and warfare, J-INNOVATECH on Japanese industrialisation) do not study business influence on policy.
notes: ABSENCE CLAIM: no project in the corpus researches efforts by businesses, firms, corporations or industry to influence the policies or regulations adopted by governments in the nineteenth century - neither in project.objective nor in any report_text section. PARENT AND EDIT: parent vec-15 'Which EU-funded projects study how companies and business groups try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt?' (L3 survey, 16 gold). One thing changed: the period, by inserting 'nineteenth-century' before the actor and putting the verbs in the past tense. Actor, action and target are the parent's, word for word. SUBTYPE FIT: zero-match, not data-absent - the facet (what a project studies, as stated in its own free text) is exactly what the parent question is answered from, and the parent returns 16 projects on it; what is missing is the instance, a nineteenth-century case. Not false-presupposition: the question presupposes nothing that the data contradicts, it simply has no members. NON-SQL PROOF - semantic sweep: search_corpus(question text, condition='pooled', k=20) over lexical, dense, hybrid and hybrid_rerank (index be84cbad9182) returned 38 distinct projects; every one adjudicated OFF-TOPIC, in two clean families. (a) Business influence on policy, but present-day: 705677 BUSWEL, 834253 TRASC, 865165 CORPORATOCRACY (all parent gold), 101026008 REGTRUST, 870722 TiGRE, 789013 OCIAN, 793639 PEDAS, 846270 PARTOWNEU, 747947 EU-Drones, 101033472 Tran-Reg, 639084 LEGALARCHITECTURES, 709386 SRR, 660245 GLONEXACO, 674888 TAX4INNO, 649351 IIT, 789461 SCOM, 727524 ENABLE.EU, 817619 AURES II, 101000216 Code Re-farm, 861034 MARKETS, 786641 SHERPA, 843825 FINGOV, 649456 ENLIGHTEN, 892444 EUDIC, 947654 IDED. (b) Nineteenth-century, but not about business influencing policy: 850742 T-MIGRANTS (theatre migrants), 648429 TRANSPOP (popular politics and ordinary people's mobilisation, 1789-1914 - the actor is the public, not business), 752163 WARCAP (fiscal capacity and warfare 1789-1913), 805098 J-INNOVATECH (Japan's industrial technical culture 1800-1885), 757291 CALLIOPE (parliamentary oratory and empire), 101022204 INVCULTURALDIPLO (cultural diplomacy 1870-1940, states not firms), 750690 GASAC, 101026870 MIRMINT, 793204 USPAIN, 840686 FED, 101027394 HuDig19 (all literary/cultural history), 693512 GEPPS (twentieth-century economic unions), 892383 RESCATA (Amazon ecology, retrieval noise). No candidate combines the two, which is the shape the near-miss requires: the retrieval stack returns plausible neighbours on both sides of the missing cell rather than nothing at all. NON-SQL PROOF - reads: three period-marked candidates found by SQL sweeps were read in full and rejected. 795823 OilandEmp ('British oil imperialism and the making of the modern Middle East, c.1901-c.1935') is early twentieth century and argues that 'british state and business interests were at the forefront of this new coercive interventionism' - joint state-business imperial expansion abroad, not business influence on domestic policy, and the wrong century. 695573 COLOUR (racialization of nineteenth-century indentured migrant labour) contains no policy-influence claim. 101025880 PETITIA studies Dutch merchants petitioning the Amsterdam city council - the closest thing in the corpus to the asked-for research, and explicitly seventeenth century ('predating the nineteenth century'). REMAINING DOUBT, disclosed: 833834 Water-Cultures ('The Water Cultures of Italy, 1500-1900') is the one row of the widest sweep. Its work-stream list includes 'the efforts of social actors, including water companies, municipalities, private entrepreneurs, technicians and users, to regulate access, use and distribution of water in 19th-century italian cities'. It was adjudicated OFF-TOPIC because the project is a social and cultural history of human-water interaction and the stream describes participation in water provision and management, not an effort to influence policies or regulations that a government adopts; a stricter reader could argue it is a marginal match.
